articles.title: New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

articles.title: A star's 'obliquity' likely has little impact on a given planet's habitability
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumstellar disk that surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar-type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given star's initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

articles.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
articles.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

articles.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.
